title: 1 Chronicles 7:14–29
context: This unit gives the descendants of Joseph: Manasseh (7:14–19) and Ephraim (7:20–29). The Manasseh list is compressed, and the family relationships are not always easy to follow. It mentions Zelophehad, whose daughters are named in Numbers 27:1 and Joshua 17:3. The Ephraim list includes a rare narrative: men of Gath killed some of Ephraim’s sons in a livestock raid, Ephraim mourned, and a new son was named Beriah because of the trouble in his house (7:21–23). The text does not say when this happened. A daughter, Sheerah, is credited with building Beth Horon (7:24), and the line runs down to Joshua son of Nun (7:27). Several of the settlements listed in 7:28–29 also appear in the boundary descriptions of Joshua 16–17. Both traditions read the unit as shared ground: God’s people include grief and loss as well as strength, and the line of Joshua reminds readers how God gave Israel the land.

verses.text: The sons of Manasseh: Asriel, whom his concubine the Aramitess bore. She bore Machir the father of Gilead.
verses.arminianNotes: Manasseh’s line begins with Asriel and with Machir, born of an Aramean concubine, “the father of Gilead.” Arminian readers note that the genealogy openly includes a foreign mother, reflecting the mixed realities of Israel’s family history without hiding them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the inclusion of an Aramean mother and see God’s purposes running through unexpected family lines. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as honest family history and as one of many places where Scripture shows outsiders woven into the story of God’s people.

verses.text: Machir took a wife of Huppim and Shuppim, whose sister’s name was Maacah. The name of the second was Zelophehad; and Zelophehad had daughters.
verses.arminianNotes: Machir marries, and the verse mentions Zelophehad, who “had daughters.” Arminian readers recall Numbers 27:1, where these daughters came forward to ask for an inheritance. Their initiative and God’s favorable answer show a God who hears and responds to his people’s requests.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also recall Zelophehad’s daughters (Numbers 27:1; Joshua 17:3) and see God’s justice providing for families without sons. Shared ground: both traditions read the brief mention as a reminder that God’s law made room for women’s inheritance, and that the Chronicler remembered it.

verses.text: Maacah the wife of Machir bore a son, and she named him Peresh. The name of his brother was Sheresh; and his sons were Ulam and Rakem.
verses.arminianNotes: Maacah, Machir’s wife, bears Peresh, whose brother is Sheresh, with sons Ulam and Rakem. Arminian readers note that the record names the mother who gave the son his name. Women appear in these lists as real participants in Israel’s family history.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the naming of Maacah and the continuation of Machir’s line. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of Manasseh’s family record, with no doctrinal dispute raised, and both note the Chronicler’s attention to mothers as well as fathers.

verses.text: The sons of Ulam: Bedan. These were the sons of Gilead the son of Machir, the son of Manasseh.
verses.arminianNotes: Ulam’s son Bedan is named, and the verse sums up “the sons of Gilead the son of Machir, the son of Manasseh.” Arminian readers note the summary that ties the generations together and anchors each family in its tribal identity within the covenant people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the summary as the Chronicler’s way of keeping the lines clear for a community that needed to know its place in Israel. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a genealogical summary and see in it God’s faithfulness from one generation to the next.

verses.text: His sister Hammolecheth bore Ishhod, Abiezer, and Mahlah.
verses.arminianNotes: Hammolecheth, a sister, bears Ishhod, Abiezer, and Mahlah. Arminian readers note that Gideon’s father is called an Abiezrite (Judges 6:11), which many connect with this Abiezer, though the text here does not mention Gideon. The list preserves the roots of families that would matter in Israel’s story.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the possible link to Gideon’s clan and the naming of a woman as the mother of this line. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of Manasseh’s record and are cautious about drawing more connections than the Chronicler states.

verses.text: The sons of Shemida were Ahian, Shechem, Likhi, and Aniam.
verses.arminianNotes: Shemida’s sons are named: Ahian, Shechem, Likhi, and Aniam. Arminian readers note that the name Shechem also belongs to a well-known town in the region, though the text does not link them here. The list completes the brief record of Manasseh’s families.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise treat the verse as a simple list of names. Shared ground: both traditions read it as genealogical detail without theological controversy, and both affirm that the preservation of such names reflects God’s care for each family among his people.

verses.text: The sons of Ephraim: Shuthelah, Bered his son, Tahath his son, Eleadah his son, Tahath his son,
verses.arminianNotes: Ephraim’s line begins, generation by generation: Shuthelah, Bered, Tahath, Eleadah, Tahath. Arminian readers note the father-to-son pattern, which suggests a line of descent traced toward a goal. Each generation had to take up its own calling before God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this line will lead to Joshua son of Nun (7:27), showing God preparing a leader long before his time. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the start of Ephraim’s line and see in it the continuity of God’s purposes across generations.

verses.text: Zabad his son, Shuthelah his son, Ezer, and Elead, whom the men of Gath who were born in the land killed, because they came down to take away their livestock.
verses.arminianNotes: Some of Ephraim’s sons are killed by the men of Gath while trying to take their livestock. Arminian readers note the honest record of a raid gone wrong. The genealogy does not hide failure or loss, and the sons’ deaths followed from their own risky choice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the plain record of a tragedy and the narrator’s refusal to idealize Ephraim’s family. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly, as a reminder that Israel’s history includes violence and grief, without making the incident a lesson the text does not draw.

verses.text: Ephraim their father mourned many days, and his brothers came to comfort him.
verses.arminianNotes: Ephraim mourns many days, and his brothers come to comfort him. Arminian readers note the human grief at the center of the genealogy. The verse invites compassion and shows that mourning and comfort are a proper part of life among God’s people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see real sorrow and the comfort of family. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a moving reminder that genealogies record real people who suffered loss, and both affirm that grief and consolation have a place in faithful life before God.

verses.text: He went in to his wife, and she conceived and bore a son, and he named him Beriah, because there was trouble with his house.
verses.arminianNotes: Ephraim has another son and names him Beriah, “because there was trouble with his house.” Arminian readers note that the name keeps the memory of loss alive. New life comes after tragedy, but the family does not pretend the sorrow did not happen.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God giving a new son after grief, even as the name remembers the trouble. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an honest picture of grief and continuing life, and both see in it God’s mercy in sustaining a family through loss.

verses.text: His daughter was Sheerah, who built Beth Horon the lower and the upper, and Uzzen Sheerah.
verses.arminianNotes: Ephraim’s daughter Sheerah builds Beth Horon, lower and upper, and Uzzen Sheerah. Arminian readers note the remarkable recognition of a woman as a builder of towns. The Chronicler credits her achievement plainly, showing that women took active roles in Israel’s history.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note this unusual tribute to a woman’s work. Beth Horon appears in Ephraim’s boundary (Joshua 16:3, 5). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as honoring Sheerah’s achievement and as evidence that God’s people were built through the labor of women as well as men.

verses.text: Rephah was his son, Resheph his son, Telah his son, Tahan his son,
verses.arminianNotes: The line continues: Rephah, Resheph, Telah, Tahan. Arminian readers note the steady succession, which carries the story forward toward Joshua. Each name represents a generation that lived and served within the people of God, though nothing more is said of them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the line moving toward its goal in Joshua (7:27). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a link in the chain of generations, and both affirm that God’s purposes advance through ordinary lives whose stories are not told.

verses.text: Ladan his son, Ammihud his son, Elishama his son,
verses.arminianNotes: Ladan, Ammihud, and Elishama follow. Arminian readers note that an Elishama son of Ammihud appears as a leader of Ephraim in the wilderness (Numbers 1:10), though the text here does not explain the link. The genealogy connects the tribe’s past with its later leaders.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the possible connection to the wilderness leader of Ephraim and are cautious about pressing it. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the line leading to Joshua and see in it the continuity of Ephraim’s leadership under God.

verses.text: Nun his son, and Joshua his son.
verses.arminianNotes: The line reaches “Nun his son, and Joshua his son.” Arminian readers note that the genealogy ends with the leader who brought Israel into the land. Joshua’s faithful leadership is remembered as part of Ephraim’s heritage and as an example to the returned community.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in Joshua the climax of the line and a reminder that God raised up leaders to fulfill his promise of the land. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as connecting the post-exilic community with the conquest, when God gave Israel the land he had promised.

verses.text: Their possessions and settlements were Bethel and its towns, and eastward Naaran, and westward Gezer with its towns; Shechem also and its towns, to Azzah and its towns;
verses.arminianNotes: Ephraim’s possessions include Bethel, Naaran, Gezer, Shechem, and Azzah, with their towns. Arminian readers note that the record ties the tribe to its land. Israel’s life with God was lived in real places, received as a gift and held in responsibility.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the list of settlements as a reminder of God’s faithfulness in giving the land. Several of these places also appear in Joshua 16. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a record of the inheritance God gave and as a link between the genealogy and the land.

verses.text: and by the borders of the children of Manasseh, Beth Shean and its towns, Taanach and its towns, Megiddo and its towns, and Dor and its towns. The children of Joseph the son of Israel lived in these.
verses.arminianNotes: Manasseh’s border towns include Beth Shean, Taanach, Megiddo, and Dor, where “the children of Joseph” lived. Arminian readers note that Joshua 17:11 names the same towns. The verse sums up Joseph’s inheritance in the land of promise.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the connection to Joshua 17:11 and see God’s promise to Joseph’s descendants fulfilled in the land. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as closing the record of Joseph’s tribes with their settlements, a reminder of God’s faithfulness in giving the land.
